raw_case_text:
A 3-month-old girl was referred to our hospital with a suspicion of Langerhans cell histiocytosis. She was hospitalized for pneumonia at the fifteenth day of birth followed by recurrent and treatment resistant cervical lymphadenopathies with high CRP levels. She was the first child of a consanguineous family. She had bilateral cervical lymphadenopathies and maculopapular skin eruptions over body and legs on admission. Laboratory investigations revealed anemia, leukocytosis, high CRP level (12 mg/dL), and hypergammaglobulinemia. Histological findings of the skin biopsy and lymph node excision were reported as granulomatous inflammation and necrotizing granulomatous lymphadenitis, respectively. Meanwhile, oxidative burst activity ("Phagoburst" kit, Glycotope, Biotechnology) was insufficient (FMLP 9%, PMA 9%, and opsonized E. Coli 4%; normal values 1-10%, 98-100%, and 97-100%, resp.) leading to a probable diagnosis of CGD later confirmed with mutation analysis disclosing a "homozygous autosomal recessive c.369 + 1G>A mutation" in CYBA gene-  p22phox.
She was admitted again with tachypnea with coarse lung sounds relevant to acute pneumonia at 30 months of age. She had anemia (Hb: 8.9 g/dL), leukocytosis (16800/mm3), and high CRP (3 mg/dL) and ESR (60 mm/hr) levels. CXR showed bilateral extensive infiltrations especially prominent in left upper lobe (Figure 3). Thorax CT revealed pneumonic consolidations with calcifications (Figure 3). These findings were interpreted in favor of tuberculosis (TB) although objective mycobacterial evidence was absent (PPD 9 mm, gastric fluid acid-fast bacilli and PCR negative). Three-drug combination therapy (isoniazid, rifampicin, and pyrazinamide) was initiated. Echocardiography showed pericardial thickening which was also evaluated as TB sequela.
Despite treatment, her clinical condition worsened in a two-month period. Extensive lymph node enlargements in mediastinum and around pericardium reaching to 3 cm in diameter, some showing central necrosis, were recorded in the new thorax CT (Figure 3). During hospitalization, she developed right congestive heart failure signs, fine crackles in lungs, and increased oxygen need. Echocardiography showed findings compatible with pulmonary hypertension, diastolic dysfunction, and constrictive pericarditis (Figure 4). Emergency pericardiectomy was performed. Aspergillus fumigatus was cultured in pericardial fluid and blood Aspergillus antigen was positive for the first time. Parenteral caspofungin and voriconazole infusions were initiated in combination for antifungal therapy. Histological interpretation of the pericardial sample was reported as granulomatous pericarditis.
Fever and respiratory distress continued and thorax CT revealed an abscess of 4.5 x 1.7 cm diameter in left lung inferior lobe, two weeks after the pericardiectomy (Figure 5). The abscess was drained and drainage material culture was positive for Aspergillus fumigatus (Figure 5). Granulocyte transfusions were applied for the subsequent days and fever subsided gradually in a few days. She was discharged with oral voriconazole after her condition stabilized with parenteral antifungal therapy for one month. Blood Aspergillus antigen was still positive in low titers.
Two weeks later, she was brought to emergency department with left hemiparesis, left central facial paralysis, and fever. Glasgow Coma Scale was 12, motor strength was 2/5 in left upper and lower extremities, and left plantar response was abnormal in neurological examination. A hypodense lesion at the level of right basal ganglia was interpreted as acute ischemic infarction in cranial CT (Figure 6). Diffusional restriction consistent with acute ischemia in right basal ganglia and cerebral, cerebellar millimetric enhancing foci consistent with aspergillosis were reported in cranial and diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (Figure 6). In MR angiography, right middle cerebral artery was occluded from M2 segment to end which was also associated with Aspergillus infection (Figure 6). Voriconazole, amphotericin B, vancomycin, and meropenem were started. Intravenous immunoglobulin, 1 gr/kg/day, was given for two days. Fever was controlled and her general condition improved. Acetylsalicylic acid treatment was commenced to prevent further infarction.
Neurological findings regressed with decreased facial asymmetry and increased motor strength in the follow-up. Parenteral antifungal treatment was continued for two months and she was discharged with oral voriconazole and negative blood Aspergillus antigen. The ischemic lesion in the right basal ganglia showed chronicity and appeared as cystic encephalomalacia; most of the cerebral/cerebellar foci were smaller than before and some disappeared in the control MRI five months after the initial evaluation (Figure 7). Due to the severe course of her disease, HSCT was planned and due to the lack of full matched relative, an unrelated donor search is initiated.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 30-month-old girl with autosomal recessive p22phox chronic granulomatous disease presented with tachypnea and acute pneumonia progressing to constrictive pericarditis and lung abscess, followed 2 weeks after discharge by fever, left hemiparesis, and left central facial palsy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Initially diagnosed in infancy with autosomal recessive CYBA (p22phox) chronic granulomatous disease after presenting at 3 months of age with neonatal pneumonia, maculopapular rash, and recurrent necrotizing granulomatous cervical lymphadenitis, the child was readmitted at 30 months of age with tachypnea and bilateral pneumonic consolidations. Empirical 3-drug anti-tuberculosis therapy failed, and over 2 months she developed necrotic mediastinal/pericardial lymphadenopathy, right heart failure from constrictive Aspergillus fumigatus pericarditis, and a left lower lobe Aspergillus abscess. Two weeks after discharge on oral voriconazole, she re-presented with acute fever, left central facial paralysis, and left hemiparesis due to a right MCA mycotic occlusion and multifocal brain microabscesses.
subjective.past_medical_history: Autosomal recessive chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) confirmed by defective phagocyte oxidative burst (Phagoburst: fMLP 9%, PMA 9%, opsonized E. coli 4%) and homozygous CYBA c.369+1G>A (p22phox) splice-site mutation; neonatal pneumonia at day 15 of life; recurrent granulomatous cervical lymphadenitis at 3 months of age; born to consanguineous parents.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for tachypnea, persistent fever, right heart failure symptoms, and subsequent acute left-sided weakness and facial asymmetry.

objective.physical_examination: At 3 months: bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy and maculopapular rash over the trunk and legs. At 30 months: tachypnea and coarse breath sounds, progressing over 2 months to fine pulmonary crackles, increased oxygen requirement, and signs of right-sided congestive heart failure. On readmission 2 weeks post-discharge: febrile, GCS 12, left central facial nerve palsy, left upper and lower extremity hemiparesis (2/5 motor strength), and extensor left plantar response.
objective.routine_investigations: At 30 months: hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL, WBC 16,800/mm3, CRP 3 mg/dL, ESR 60 mm/h, PPD 9 mm, and negative gastric aspirate AFB smears and MTB PCR. Chest X-ray showed extensive bilateral infiltrates (prominent in the left upper lobe). Echocardiography initially showed pericardial thickening, progressing to pulmonary hypertension, diastolic dysfunction, and constrictive pericarditis.
objective.advanced_workup: Thoracic CT at 30 months showed pneumonic consolidations with calcifications, progressing at 2 months to 3-cm necrotic mediastinal and paracardiac lymphadenopathy and, 2 weeks post-pericardiectomy, a 4.5 x 1.7 cm left lower lobe lung abscess. Emergency pericardiectomy histopathology showed granulomatous pericarditis, and cultures of both pericardial fluid and drained left lower lobe lung abscess fluid grew Aspergillus fumigatus, accompanied by positive serum Aspergillus galactomannan antigenemia. Upon neurological readmission, cranial CT, diffusion MRI, and MR angiography revealed an acute right basal ganglia ischemic infarction secondary to right middle cerebral artery (M2 segment) occlusion alongside multiple millimetric enhancing cerebral and cerebellar foci of CNS aspergillosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Proven disseminated invasive aspergillosis (Aspergillus fumigatus) presenting sequentially as pneumonia, constrictive granulomatous pericarditis, left lower lobe lung abscess, and angioinvasive right MCA occlusion with right basal ganglia infarction and multifocal cerebral/cerebellar microabscesses in a 30-month-old child with homozygous CYBA (p22phox) chronic granulomatous disease, confirmed by pericardial fluid and lung abscess cultures, positive serum Aspergillus galactomannan, pericardiectomy histopathology, and brain MRI/MRA. Treated with emergency pericardiectomy, percutaneous lung abscess drainage, granulocyte transfusions, combination intravenous voriconazole plus caspofungin (later voriconazole plus amphotericin B, IVIG, and aspirin during the CNS stroke/abscess phase), and maintenance oral voriconazole, achieving galactomannan clearance, neurological motor recovery, and MRI regression at 5 months while awaiting unrelated-donor allogeneic HSCT.
